newsitem.title: USA: ALPINE SKIING-VON GRUENIGEN WINS GIANT, ALPHAND EYES OVERALL.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-VON GRUENIGEN WINS GIANT, ALPHAND EYES OVERALL.

text.p: World Cup giant slalom champion Michael von Gruenigen of Switzerland charged to victory at the World Cup Finals on Saturday as Frenchman Luc Alphand moved tantalizingly close to taking the overall title.

Von Gruenigen, who also won the world championship this year, claimed his fourth win of the World Cup season with a sizzling second run that put him nearly one second ahead of Austrian Rainer Salzgeber, the first-leg leader.

Celebrating almost as hard as von Gruenigen despite not racing Saturday was Alphand, who accepted claps on the back from Italian star Alberto Tomba and his Austrian rivals after a seventh-place finish virtually eliminated Norway's Kjetil Andre Aamodt from contention for the overall crown.

Alphand will become France's first overall champion in 29 years -- the first since Jean-Claude Killy in 1968 -- unless Aamodt, ranked eighth in the discipline, wins Sunday's season-ending slalom or finishes second. The Norwegian has finished 10th, 11th and 15th in his last three slaloms.
"Today I got a lot of support from Austrians, who are usually my big rivals," said Alphand, who leads Aamodt by 70 points after four Austrians finished ahead of the Norwegian.
"I was as nervous as if I was racing today. but the World Cup is not over. This was not a victory -- only a step towards victory."
A second run that was nearly a full second better than anyone in the elite field carried von Gruenigen to victory in a combined time of two minutes, 18.58 seconds. Salzgeber finished in 2:19.57.
Taking third place behind Salzgeber was Austrian Andreas Schifferer, winner of Thursday's Super-G, who clocked 2:19.57, 0.31 of a second ahead of Italy's Patrick Holzer.

"I had a great season last year and this year also," said the 27-year-old von Gruenigen. "I won the world champion and I showed I'm a worthy champion. Now I'm looking forward to Nagano (Olympics) and another great season."
Much of the tension in the race centred on Aamodt, who needed a strong showing to close the points gap with Alphand.

But the 25-year-old Norwegian struggled with the technically difficult turning section towards the end of the course and finished tied with Swede Fredrik Nyberg at 2:20.92 behind Austrians Hermann Maier and Josef Strobl.
"I risked everything but it was not good enough," said Aamodt, the 1994 World Cup champion. "My chances are not gone until the end, but I have to do a season's best in slalom."

Alphand, hoping to become the first speed specialist ever to win the overall crown, sabotaged a psychological ploy by his coaches, who put his name on the giant slalom start list in hopes of worrying Aamodt.

But Alphand, who has not raced a technical event in six years, never intended to race and stayed in bed Saturday morning after getting back to the hotel at 3 a.m. after attending a Colorado Avalanche National Hockey League game Friday night in Denver.
Alphand's presence on the hill was not needed.
With Austrian coaches yelling at Alphand that he would have to "pay up!" for the help they gave him in the giant slalom, the 31-year-old Frenchman allowed himself a laugh.
"I was hoping that maybe I'd only have to buy a few beers for the Austrians," said Alphand. "But it looks more like steaks and whiskey. It's going to be expensive for me."
Still, the Frenchman cautioned that the overall race was not done.
"It is not finished," he said. "When mathematics say there still is a chance for Aamodt, it's not over for me.
"This winter in slalom he wasn't so good and he needs a victory or second. But he is a fighter."
